quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word has a nasal in the middle and another at the end. Focus on the middle one: do your lips close for it, or does your tongue tip lift?
quests.explanation: 'Lemon' has /m/ in the middle: the lips press together while voiced air flows through the nose, and the weak last syllable then ends with /n/. If the lips don't close, the middle blurs into a second /n/ and you get 'lenon'.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'le-', close your lips and hum through your nose, then relax into the weak 'un' ending.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: After the first vowel, do your lips stay open, or do they come together?
quests.explanation: 'Penny' has /n/ in the middle: the tongue tip rises to the ridge and voiced air passes through the nose while the lips stay apart. Closing the lips gives /m/ and 'pemmy'. The double N in the spelling is still one sound.
quests.mouthPosition: Between the two vowels, keep the tongue tip on the ridge and let the hum run out through the nose; lips stay apart.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Say the word and hold the last sound. If you rested a fingertip on your lips, would they be pressed together?
quests.explanation: 'Swim' ends in /m/: the lips close and the voiced air exits through the nose, so the word finishes in a hum. Lifting the tongue tip gives 'swin'. The closing lips are the last thing a listener can see and hear.
quests.mouthPosition: Finish by closing both lips and letting the hum run out through your nose. Keep the tongue relaxed.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Say the word and hold the ending. Is the hum coming from the back of your mouth or the front?
quests.explanation: 'Sing' ends in /ŋ/. The back of the tongue rises to the soft palate and the hum passes through the nose; the letter G doesn't get a sound of its own. If the tongue tip lifts instead, you get 'sin'.
quests.mouthPosition: Raise the back of your tongue to touch the soft palate and hum through your nose. Keep the tongue tip down behind your lower teeth.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Freeze at the end of the word. Is the tip of your tongue touching the ridge, or is the back of the tongue raised?
quests.explanation: 'Win' ends in /n/: tongue tip on the ridge behind the upper teeth, voiced air through the nose. Lifting the back of the tongue instead gives 'wing'. The ending is the only thing separating the two words.
quests.mouthPosition: Park your tongue tip on the ridge behind your upper teeth as the word closes, and hum through your nose.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: There are silent letters here. Ignore the spelling and feel where your tongue is as the word finishes.
quests.explanation: 'Wrong' begins with /r/ (the W is silent) and ends with /ŋ/, made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate. No /g/ is released. Ending with the tongue tip would give 'ron', a different word.
quests.mouthPosition: End with the back of your tongue lifted to the soft palate, humming through your nose, with the tongue tip low.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: In the middle of the word, the sound is a single hum. Is it made with the tongue tip or the back of the tongue?
quests.explanation: 'Singer' has /ŋ/ in the middle, the same sound as at the end of 'sing', and no /g/ is added, so it's 'sing-er', not 'sing-ger'. The back of the tongue stays up through the hum, then drops for the weak final 'er'. A tongue-tip /n/ would give 'sinner', a completely different word.
quests.mouthPosition: Raise the back of your tongue to the soft palate on 'sing-', hum through your nose, then lower it into the weak 'er'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The letter N sits before a K in the spelling. Where does your tongue actually go on the way to the K?
quests.explanation: 'Monkey' has /ŋ/ before the /k/. The back of the tongue is already raised for the /k/, so the nasal is made in the same place. Using a tongue-tip /n/ forces the tongue to jump forward and back, which sounds hesitant. Let the back of the tongue stay up.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'mu-', raise the back of your tongue to the soft palate, hum through your nose, then release into the 'k' and the final 'ee'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The nasal comes right before a D. Where is the tongue tip: on the ridge, or is the back of the tongue raised?
quests.explanation: 'Candy' has /n/ in the middle, made with the tongue tip on the ridge, exactly where the following /d/ is made. The tongue doesn't need to move between them. A back-of-tongue nasal would sound like 'cang-dy'.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'ca-', touch your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth, hum through your nose, then release into the 'd' and the final 'ee'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Say the first sound and check whether your tongue tip touches the ridge behind your teeth. Should it?
quests.explanation: 'Red' starts with /r/: the tongue is pulled back, its sides hug the upper back teeth, and the tip points up without touching anything, while the lips round slightly. /l/ presses the tip onto the ridge, and touching gives 'led'.
quests.mouthPosition: Pull your tongue back and up, keep the tip from touching anything, and round your lips slightly. Voice on throughout.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Breathe in through your mouth while you hold the first sound. Do you feel cool air along the sides of your tongue?
quests.explanation: 'Light' starts with /l/: the tongue tip presses on the ridge behind the upper teeth and voiced air flows around the sides. That's why cool air shows up along the sides of the tongue when you breathe in. /r/ has no tip contact and would give 'right'.
quests.mouthPosition: Press your tongue tip firmly against the ridge behind your upper teeth, voice on, and let air escape around the sides of the tongue.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word has one liquid sound in the middle. Does the tongue tip touch the ridge, or hover in the air?
quests.explanation: 'Yellow' has /l/ in the middle: the tongue tip touches the ridge briefly and then drops into the final 'oh'. The word starts with /j/ and has no /r/ at all. Learners sometimes swap in /r/ mid-word and say 'yerrow'.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'ye-', press your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth, then drop it quickly into the final 'oh'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Hold the first sound and pinch your nose. Does anything change?
quests.explanation: 'Leaf' starts with /l/: voiced air flows out through the mouth around the sides of the tongue, so pinching your nose changes nothing. /n/ sends the air through the nose and would make 'neaf'. The tongue tip sits in the same place for both, so the nose is the giveaway.
quests.mouthPosition: Press your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth, voice on, and let the air flow around the sides and out of your mouth.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Hold the first sound and rest a fingertip on the side of your nose. Do you feel any vibration?
quests.explanation: 'Need' begins with /n/: tongue tip on the ridge with voiced air going through the nose. /l/ keeps the air inside the mouth and would give 'lead'. In some languages the two are interchangeable; in English they change the word.
quests.mouthPosition: Touch your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth and hum through your nose, then release into the 'ee'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: At the end of the word, does your tongue tip stay up on the ridge with air escaping around the sides, or does the sound go through your nose?
quests.explanation: 'Feel' ends in /l/: the tongue tip touches the ridge and the air flows around the sides of the tongue. Ending with /n/ gives 'fean', which isn't a word, so listeners have to guess. Lift the tip and hold it for a beat.
quests.mouthPosition: Straight after the vowel, lift your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth and hold it there with your voice on.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The tongue does the work here. Can you feel it pulled back, with its sides pressing on your upper back teeth?
quests.explanation: 'Rain' begins with /r/: the tongue pulls back and up with the sides touching the upper back teeth, while the lips are only slightly rounded. /w/ is made mostly by the lips, so the tongue stays low and you'd hear 'wain'. The tongue's retraction is what makes an /r/.
quests.mouthPosition: Pull your tongue back with the tip curled up but not touching anything, sides against your upper back teeth, lips slightly rounded.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Watch your lips: do they gather tightly and then spring open? What is your tongue doing meanwhile?
quests.explanation: 'Wet' begins with /w/: the lips round tightly, the back of the tongue lifts a little, and the lips spring open into the vowel. /r/ would pull the tongue back and give 'ret'. The lip movement is the visible sign.
quests.mouthPosition: Round and push your lips forward tightly, then open them quickly into 'et'. The tongue stays low and relaxed.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Between the weak first syllable and the stressed 'ound', what does your tongue do? Is it pulled back, or are your lips doing the work?
quests.explanation: 'Around' has /r/ at the start of the stressed syllable, after the weak first 'a'. The tongue pulls back to make the /r/ before the vowel. Rounding the lips instead gives /w/, which can sound like 'a-wound'.
quests.mouthPosition: After the short 'uh', pull your tongue back with the tip lifted but not touching, then open into the stressed 'ow' vowel.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: In the middle of the word, do your lips round forward, or does your lip touch your teeth?
quests.explanation: 'Away' has /w/ in the middle: the lips round and open quickly into the stressed 'ay', with no lip-teeth contact. Adding /v/ would give 'avay', which sounds like a different word.
quests.mouthPosition: Once the short 'uh' is said, round your lips tightly and open into 'ay'. Keep your teeth off your lip.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle consonant: teeth on lip with a buzz, or lips rounded with no contact?
quests.explanation: 'River' has /v/ in the middle: the teeth rest on the lower lip and voiced air buzzes through. /w/ would give 'riwer'. A buzz between two vowels is easy to skip, so be deliberate about it.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'ri-', rest your top teeth on your bottom lip with your voice on, buzz for a beat, and finish with the weak 'er'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Notice whether your lower lip touches your teeth as the word begins.
quests.explanation: 'Wine' begins with /w/, whereas 'vine' would begin with /v/. The rounded lips don't touch the teeth at all. This pair is worth practising for restaurants and shops, where the mix-up actually happens.
quests.mouthPosition: Round your lips as though blowing out a candle, then open them into 'ine'. Your teeth stay away from your lip.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Is there a blocked moment at the start, or does the sound glide smoothly into the vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Yes' starts with /j/: the middle of the tongue rises toward the hard palate and glides straight into the vowel, with no closure. /dʒ/ adds a seal and a buzz and would give 'jess'. If you feel a seal on the roof of your mouth, it isn't /j/.
quests.mouthPosition: Raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth, as if starting to say 'ee', and glide straight into 'es'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Feel the roof of your mouth behind the ridge. Does the tongue seal there and release, or just glide near it?
quests.explanation: 'Jump' starts with /dʒ/: the tongue seals against the roof behind the ridge and releases into a buzzy hush. /j/ only glides near the roof and would give 'yump'. The seal separates them.
quests.mouthPosition: Press the front of your tongue up behind the ridge and sound your voice before you release; a soft buzzy hush follows, then 'ump'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Between 'on' and the weak last syllable, does the tongue seal against the roof, or glide up close to it?
quests.explanation: 'Onion' has /j/ in the middle, spelled with an I: the tongue glides up toward the hard palate between the 'n' and the weak vowel. Sealing gives /dʒ/ and 'unjun'. Think 'un-yun'.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'un-', raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof as if for 'ee', and glide into the weak 'un'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word starts with WH, but only the ending matters. Hold the last sound: can you feel air passing over the sides of your tongue?
quests.explanation: 'Wheel' ends in /l/: the tongue tip lifts to the ridge and holds while voiced air flows around the sides. Ending with /n/ gives 'ween'. The long vowel before it makes a small glide as the tongue moves up.
quests.mouthPosition: Following the 'ee', lift your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth and hold, voice on, air flowing around the sides.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: At the end of the word, feel whether the air goes through your nose or around the sides of your tongue.
quests.explanation: 'Seen' ends in /n/: the tongue tip on the ridge and voiced air through the nose. /l/ would give 'seal'. Both endings use the same tongue position, so the airflow route is the difference.
quests.mouthPosition: Finish with your tongue tip touching the ridge behind your upper teeth and hum through your nose.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE FIRST CONSONANT SOUND IN THE FINAL CLUSTER
quests.hint: After the vowel, the tongue tip has to go somewhere before the lips close. Does it touch the ridge, or hover?
quests.explanation: 'Help' has /l/ before the final /p/: the tongue tip touches the ridge right after the vowel, then the lips close. Skip the touch and you'd get 'hep', and with /r/ you'd hear 'herp'. The touch is short, but it's needed.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'he-', touch your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth briefly, then close your lips for the 'p'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Which does the work: lip rounding, or the tongue pulling back?
quests.explanation: 'Right' begins with /r/: the tongue pulls back and up without touching the roof, and the lips round only slightly. /w/ uses tightly rounded lips and would give 'white'. The tongue's retraction is the key.
quests.mouthPosition: Pull your tongue back with the tip lifted but not touching, and round your lips slightly before opening into 'ight'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word ends with the letters NG. Where does your tongue finish: tip or back?
quests.explanation: 'Along' ends in /ŋ/: the back of the tongue lifts to the soft palate and the sound hums through the nose; the G isn't pronounced. Using /n/ instead would give 'alon', which sounds like a different word.
quests.mouthPosition: Straight after the stressed 'o', raise the back of your tongue to the soft palate and hum through your nose. No release.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word contains both a lip nasal and a tongue-tip nasal. Focus on the very first sound: do your lips close?
quests.explanation: 'Mind' begins with /m/ and finishes with /n/ plus /d/. The start closes the lips; the /n/ inside the word uses the tongue tip. Keeping them separate is what lets listeners hear the word cleanly from the first sound.
quests.mouthPosition: Close your lips, hum through your nose, then open into 'ind' and finish with the tongue tip on the ridge.
